newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian court may ask to delay report on minister.
newsitem.headline: Belgian court may ask to delay report on minister.

text.p: Belgium's top court may ask parliament on Monday for more time to investigate child sex allegations against Deputy Prime Minister Elio di Rupo, political sources said at the weekend.
Such a move would prolong the agony of Belgium's coalition government, that has been virtually paralysed since the allegations first surfaced three weeks ago.
The parliament on November 21 asked the Cour de Cassation, the country's highest court, to investigate allegations that Di Rupo had sex with under age boys, and to report back by December 9.
Di Rupo denies the allegations, insisting that he has never had anything to do with paedophilia, and some senior politicians have spoken of political machinations.
The court report is expected to state whether there is enough evidence to warrant indicting the number two in the Belgian centre-left government.
But on Wednesday the Brussels prosecutor general sent new information about the Di Rupo investigation to the Cour de Cassation, leaving the court just two working days to study it.
"There is a possibility that the Cour de Cassation will ask parliament for more time," a parliament official told Reuters.
On Friday, two days before the report was due, Di Rupo had still not been heard by the court, but his spokesman told Reuters the court was under no obligation to hear the minister.
"If the court considers the allegations are not serious enough, it may decide not to hear him," he said on Friday.
The Belgian press has questioned the reliability of the only identified witness against Di Rupo.
If the Cour de Cassation does not ask for extra time, parliament has three options.

It can decide the allegations against Di Rupo are unfounded and clear his name, it can decide to indict him or it can ask for yet another investigation which would have the same impact on the government as a request from the court for more time.
An indictment would mean sending Di Rupo to the Cour de Cassation for a full investigation -- a move which would end his political career.
In Belgium, only parliament can indict ministers and only the Cour de Cassation can try them.

A similar procedure brought down former NATO Secretary General Willy Claes, who was forced to resign in October 1995 after parliament indicted him over allegations of bribery when he was a Belgian economics minister in the late eighties.
If Di Rupo's name is cleared, the political world will be forced to deal with the question whether a gay man can hold a top government post.
One of the side consequences of the investigation into Di Rupo has been the exposure to the public of his homosexuality.
The chairman of francophone christian-democrat government party said last week that a minister could not be openly gay.
